plain.text: Three days after arriving in his province, Festus went up to Jerusalem. The chief priests and leaders asked him to transfer Paul to Jerusalem, planning to ambush and kill him on the way. Festus said they should come to Caesarea and bring their charges there. In Caesarea, they made many serious charges they could not prove. Paul said, "I have done nothing wrong against the law, the temple or Caesar." Festus, wanting to do the leaders a favour, asked Paul if he would go to Jerusalem to stand trial.

Paul answered, "I am now standing before Caesar's court, where I ought to be tried. I have not done any wrong to the Jews, as you very well know. If I am guilty of anything deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if the charges are not true, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!" After conferring, Festus said, "You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!"

A few days later King Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea. Festus explained Paul's case: the accusers had not charged him with any crime he expected, but had disputes about their religion and about a dead man named Jesus whom Paul claimed was alive. Agrippa said, "I would like to hear this man myself."

The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, with military leaders and important men of the city. Paul was brought in. Festus said that he had found Paul had done nothing deserving death, but since he had appealed to the Emperor, Festus needed something definite to write about him. He hoped King Agrippa could help.

summary.bigIdea: Facing an unfair trial, Paul uses his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to Caesar, which will take him to Rome.
points: Leaders plot to ambush Paul again.
Paul appeals to Caesar: "To Caesar you will go!"
Festus admits Paul has done nothing deserving death and asks King Agrippa to hear him.
summary.reflection: God had promised Paul he would testify in Rome. How do you see God working through difficult circumstances?
